title: Matthew 9:35–38
context: Jesus’ Galilean circuit—teaching, kingdom gospel, and healing—frames His compassion for harassed, shepherdless crowds. He turns disciples toward prayer: plentiful harvest, few laborers, ask the Lord of the harvest will send workers.

voices.heading: Voices from both camps
voices.intro: What older interpreters in each camp said about Jesus’ Galilean circuit—teaching, kingdom gospel, and healing—frames His compassion for harassed, shepherdless crowds.
voices.note: Quotations lightly abridged for length; wording follows standard English translations of the sources named.

arminian.quote: Because they were faint - In soul rather than in body. As sheep having no shepherd - And yet they had many teachers; they had scribes in every city. But they had none who cared for their souls, and none that were able, if they had been willing, to have wrought any deliverance.
arminian.source: Explanatory Notes upon the New Testament (on Matt 9:35–38)

reformed.quote: And Jesus went about This statement is made by way of anticipating an objection, and is intended to inform us that the whole ministry of Christ is not minutely described: for he was constantly employed in the discharge of his office; that is, in proclaiming the doctrine of salvation, and in confirming it by the addition of miracles. The gospel of the kingdom, we have already said, is a designation given to it from its effect, for in this way God gathered to himself a people sadly scattered, that he might reign in the midst of them; and, indeed, he erected his throne for the express purpose of bestowing on all his people perfect happiness.
reformed.source: Commentary on a Harmony of the Evangelists (on Matt 9:35–38)

verses.text: Jesus went about all the cities and the villages, teaching in their synagogues and preaching the Good News of the Kingdom, and healing every disease and every sickness among the people.
verses.arminianNotes:
Comprehensive mission: teach, proclaim, heal—cities and villages alike. The Good News of the Kingdom is good news announced, not mere advice.

Jesus’ pattern is the church’s model under grace—word and mercy together. The offer goes widely; hearers are summoned to respond.
verses.reformedNotes:
The King’s itinerary is exhaustive in scope and authority. Synagogue, gospel, healing—one Messiah doing the Father’s works.

“Every” disease underlines sovereignty of power, not a promise that every illness in every age ends on demand, but that none could resist Him then.

verses.text: But when he saw the multitudes, he was moved with compassion for them because they were harassed and scattered, like sheep without a shepherd.
verses.arminianNotes:
Compassion is Jesus’ gut-level mercy for people chewed up and lying down—shepherdless sheep. Jesus sees the crowds before he sends the workers.

Let His compassion shape yours. Lostness is not in doubt; the Shepherd still cares. You may come as harassed and find Him moved with mercy.
verses.reformedNotes:
Ezekiel’s shepherdless flock meets the true Shepherd’s pity. Compassion here is divine character in the flesh.

Election’s Shepherd is not cold. His pity grounds mission; chapter 10’s sending flows from this sight.

verses.text: Then he said to his disciples, “The harvest indeed is plentiful, but the laborers are few.
verses.arminianNotes:
Harvest imagery: field ready, workers scarce. Urgency without despair—opportunity outruns staffing.

Do not shrug at scarcity. The plentiful harvest implies a call to labor; disciples are responsible to care and to pray.
verses.reformedNotes:
Kingdom agriculture under the Lord’s ownership. Plentiful harvest is God’s doing; few laborers is the church’s felt need.

Scarcity of workers does not threaten God’s election; it drives dependent prayer and obedient going.

verses.text: Pray therefore that the Lord of the harvest will send out laborers into his harvest.”
verses.arminianNotes:
First response is earnest prayer to the Lord of the harvest—He owns the field and sends workers. Prayer precedes programs.

Wesleyan Arminians stress sincere petition that God would raise and send laborers, and that we remain willing to be among those sent. Undisputed: mission begins on our knees before the Lord who harvests.
verses.reformedNotes:
“Lord of the harvest” names divine ownership and authority to thrust out workers. Prayer is the appointed means.

God sends; we ask. Chapter 10 will answer this prayer in the Twelve—sovereign sending that matches compassionate seeing.
verses.keyContrast: Both urge earnest prayer for laborers. Arminians stress willing participation in a sincerely offered mission; Reformed interpreters usually emphasize that the Lord of the harvest effectually sends those He appoints, in answer to the prayers He ordains.
